items.author: powponder
items.text:
DFW’s 100° Average Is Trending Up! ☀️🔥

DFW’s current official 30-year average (1991–2020) is 20 days of 100°+ temperatures per year.

Every 10 years, that 30-year average is updated. Currently 1991-2020. The next one will cover 2001–2030.

So far, through 2026, DFW is running at roughly 23 days per year. If we finish this summer with 50 days at 100°+, DFW would only need to average about 22 days per year from 2027–2030 for the new 30-year average to finish at 23 days per year.

🔥 Bottom line: When the new climate averages come out in 2031, there’s a good chance DFW’s average number of 100° days will be higher than today’s 20 days. 

And remember we still have four more summers after this one before that new 30 year average is finalized.

I’ve had lots of questions about averages. I would expect a lot of “above averages” until the new average resets in 2031.

items.text:
FINALLY!!! There are some pretty encouraging signs showing up for LATE next weekend.

We still have to get through another stretch of September heat first, but longer range data continues to point toward a much stronger cold front pushing south into Oklahoma next weekend.

And this one could actually have some teeth.

Some of the latest guidance is showing temperatures potentially falling 15–20° or more below normal behind the front across parts of Oklahoma and Kansas. That would be a HUGE change compared to what we’re dealing with right now.

We’re still about a week away, so I wouldn’t lock onto the exact numbers just yet. Timing and just how strong the cooler air becomes will continue to move around over the next several days.

But the overall signal is definitely there.

Hang in there. Some real relief from the heat may FINALLY be on the horizon!

Rise Up Restoration

INLAND NW & N. U.S. ROCKIES RAIN CHANCES INCREASING⛰️🌧️ a slow-moving storm system
will produce widespread rain and scattered thunderstorms across eastern Washington, Idaho and Montana Sunday into Monday! The WPC has highlighted the area in an excessive rain risk, meaning isolated flash flooding is possible. One potential band of heavier rain may develop from extreme eastern Washington and the Idaho Panhandle into Montana. This includes areas around Pullman, Lewiston, Spokane, Coeur d’Alene, Kellogg and Sandpoint. Confidence remains low regarding the exact placement and intensity, but locally heavy rainfall could produce debris flows near burn scars and steep terrain, rockslides and rapid rises along small creeks and streams.

The greatest overall rainfall totals are expected across northwest and north-central Montana Sunday night into Monday. Widespread amounts of 1-3 inches are possible, with isolated totals near 4 inches. Thunderstorms across Montana could briefly produce rainfall rates of 1-2 inches per hour. Storm movement should limit the potential for widespread flooding. 

Widespread major-river flooding is not currently expected. The primary concerns are localized flash flooding, burn-scar debris flows, rockslides and minor flooding along smaller, faster-responding streams⛰️🌧️

To support employees and residents, 52 portable toilets and more than 100 handwashing stations will also be placed throughout affected areas beginning Sunday. Temporary shower and laundry locations have also been identified.

Officials continue to carefully manage the South Rim’s limited stored water supply, stressing that every gallon conserved gives crews more time and flexibility as they work toward solutions. WESTERN RAIN & FLOOD RISK SUNDAY🌧️⚠️Sunday is shaping up to be an unusually wet day across parts of the West, with rain and thunderstorms stretching from California and Arizona north through Nevada and Utah into Oregon, Washington, Idaho, Montana, Wyoming and Colorado.

The WPC has a broad risk or excessive rainfall and flooding across much of the region, with an elevated risk from southern Nevada and northwestern Arizona into southern and central Utah, where scattered flash flooding is possible.

Hurricane Marie will remain well offshore, but its deep tropical moisture will be pulled north and northeast across Southern California, the Mojave Desert, Nevada and Utah. Rain will spread across parts of Southern California Sunday, becoming heavier and more widespread farther inland. The greatest concern will be from southern Nevada-northwestern Arizona into Utah, where locally heavy rain could quickly flood washes, slot canyons, burn scars and other vulnerable terrain.

Farther north, a slow-moving upper low will produce another area of widespread showers and thunderstorms across Washington, Oregon, Idaho and Montana. Locally heavy rain is possible, particularly near the mountains and recent burn scars. Parts of the northern Rockies could receive a significant soaking through early next week.

Rain and thunderstorms will also increase across Wyoming and Colorado, while parts of Arizona and New Mexico see scattered storms capable of locally heavy rain. If you have outdoor plans for the holiday weekend, be prepared to move indoors if storms approach🌧️⚠️

items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text:
HURRICANE MARIE MOISTURE & SUNDAY FLOOD RISK🌧️🌴⚠️a significant plume of tropical moisture associated with Hurricane Marie will surge north across parts of the West on Sunday, bringing a widespread increase in rain from Southern California through Nevada and into Utah. Marie itself will remain well offshore, but its moisture is being pulled north ahead of a trough moving through the West.

The WPC has placed the region in a risk for excessive rain and localized flooding from Southern California, into southern Nevada and northwestern Arizona into southern and central Utah. This includes some particularly flash-flood-prone areas of the Southwest. The combination of unusually deep tropical moisture, disturbances moving through the region and terrain enhancement to support locally heavier rainfall. Some of the highest concern is across southwestern Utah, where slot canyons, normally dry washes and other sensitive terrain could become dangerous quickly.

Across Southern California, periods of rain and a few thunderstorms are expected, with generally moderate amounts around Los Angeles and lighter amounts near San Diego. The moisture and rainfall become more widespread farther inland toward the Mojave Desert.

Across southern Nevada, including the Las Vegas region, rain becomes more widespread Sunday. Locally heavier showers and thunderstorms could produce rapid runoff, ponding on roads and flooding of normally dry washes. The greatest flood potential extends from southern Nevada and northwestern Arizona northeastward into Utah.

The tropical moisture plume then pushes into Utah, where widespread showers and embedded thunderstorms are expected. Today marks the 30th anniversary of Hurricane Fran; on the evening of September 5th, 1996, at 830PM, Hurricane Fran made landfall near Bald Head Island. It left devastating impacts on NC; Fran developed from a Tropical wave that came off Africa and tracked across the Atlantic Ocean. Fran made landfall near Bald Head Island as a Cat 3 Hurricane with winds of 115MPH. Fran caused catastrophic damage and flooding; it was responsible for 26 deaths and was the most expensive natural disaster in NC ever at the time. Hurricane Fran brought impacts far inland with hurricane-force wind gusts into Raleigh. I spoke to some folks this month in Raleigh who remember it vividly; parts of Central North Carolina including Raleigh did not have power or running water for 1-3 weeks. It caused 4 billion dollars in damage with 750 million in the Raleigh/Wake County area alone. It remains one of the worst hurricanes to ever hit NC. A Wind gust of 105MPH occurred in Southport, a 100MPH Wind gust in Atlantic Beach, and a 79MPH wind gust in Raleigh. Fran’s easterly winds pushed a surge of water up the river basins. The storm surge reached 10 feet in Swansboro and along the Neuse River in New Bern. In Washington, the 9-foot surge up the Pamlico River. It caused a 12 foot surge along New Hanover and Pender County beaches. Parts of the state were without power for weeks, and some places were uninhabitable for months. Do you remember?

Raleigh's population has more than doubled since Hurricane Fran, and I can tell you from experience Raleigh is not ready for another major Hurricane by any means. When people ask if Hurricanes impact inland North Carolina, yes they do!  
-Ethan

A few thunderstorms are possible, and heavier showers could produce localized flooding.

By Sunday, the moisture plume stretches farther northeast across the Mojave Desert, southern Nevada, northwest Arizona and Utah. Rain and thunderstorms will become more scattered farther east, but pockets of heavier rainfall will be possible, particularly from the Mojave Desert into southern Nevada and southwest Utah. Then attention turns to next week.

Marie is forecast to gradually weaken and turn more northwest to northward while remaining hundreds of miles offshore. Another Pacific trough could eventually capture some of Marie’s remnant tropical moisture and pull it northward along the West Coast and into the Great Basin during the middle to latter part of next week.

That could bring another increase in showers and thunderstorms across portions of California and Nevada, with some of that moisture potentially reaching Oregon and even the Pacific Northwest later in the week. Exactly how far north and inland the moisture gets remains uncertain and will depend heavily on the position of the next trough.

So again, while Marie is not forecast to make landfall in California, it's tropical moisture will get pulled away from the Hurricane in multiple waves. The first arrives this weekend, followed by the potential for a second and possibly broader surge next week. This does not mean it will rain everywhere or every day, but the overall pattern continues to favor periods of unusually deep moisture across portions of the West🌀🌧️

items.author: NTXWC
items.text:
The STRONGEST El Niño EVER recorded is upon us, which will have SERIOUS effects on how our weather pattern plays out this winter.

An El Niño pattern happens when sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean become warmer than average.

This year, they are forecast to be the strongest we have *ever* seen. 

Strong El Niño winters typically feature a stronger, more active southern storm track, increasing the odds of wetter and sometimes cooler conditions across the southern U.S. 

That can mean more frequent storm systems crossing Texas and, when cold air is available, opportunities for winter storms, ice and snow. It does NOT guarantee a snowy winter, but an active subtropical jet gives us more systems capable of producing precipitation when cold air happens to be in place. 

A more active storm track means more storm energy for severe weather outbreaks as well. One unforgettable analog is the 2015-16 super El Niño. On December 26, 2015, North Texas experienced a major tornado outbreak producing 12 tornadoes, including the deadly Garland-Rowlett EF4. The outbreak killed 13 people. The 2015-16 El Niño was among the strongest on record.

Does this mean we will see widespread tornado outbreaks on the daily? Absolutely not. But going into an even stronger pattern than we've ever seen is certainly ringing alarm bells for a potentially anomalous winter across the southeast. 

Again, a strong El Niño does NOT mean tornadoes will strike your house, or a historic winter storm will dump buckets of snow on the southeast. There is no way to predict individual events. 

Think of it as potential energy storing up. This pattern will give us more storm track energy and opportunities to see frequent cold swings and severe weather outbreaks, but there is no saying in how, when, or where these specific events will play out. Only time will tell if the strongest El Niño will really live up to it's name.

COULD OKLAHOMA SEE ABOVE-NORMAL SNOWFALL THIS WINTER?

I’ve been digging through Tulsa’s snowfall history and comparing it with past El Niño winters, and there are some interesting numbers that have my attention as we look ahead to this winter.

First, Tulsa’s current 30-year normal seasonal snowfall is about 8.7 inches.

When you look back through the historical record, several El Niño winters have produced some very impressive snowfall totals in Tulsa.

1957–58: 17.2 inches
1963–64: 13.9 inches
1969–70: 20.4 inches
1972–73: 14.1 inches
1987–88: 18.2 inches
2002–03: 20.4 inches
2006–07: around 15 inches
2009–10: 22.8 inches

Those aren’t small departures from normal. Several of those winters produced roughly double Tulsa’s normal seasonal snowfall, and 2009–10 ended up being one of the snowiest winter seasons in Tulsa’s historical record.

Now, does El Niño automatically mean Oklahoma gets buried in snow?

No. And that’s important.

We’ve also had El Niño winters with very little snow. The 1997–98 winter produced only about 3.4 inches in Tulsa, and the most recent El Niño winter, 2023–24, produced only about 1.6 inches.

But El Niño can change the overall setup in a way that becomes favorable for Oklahoma.

During many El Niño winters, the southern storm track becomes more active. That can mean more systems moving across the southern United States and potentially more opportunities for precipitation across Oklahoma.

And that’s really what I’m interested in.

More opportunities.

To get a snowy winter in Oklahoma, you need storms. Then you need enough cold air available when those storms arrive.

If we can get those two ingredients to overlap several times this winter, snowfall can add up quickly.

A storm arriving with temperatures in the upper 30s gives us a cold rain.

Move that same storm into Oklahoma with temperatures below freezing and suddenly we’re talking about snow, sleet or freezing rain.

That’s why seasonal snowfall forecasting is so difficult here. The difference between a winter with 4 inches and one with 20 inches can come down to the timing of cold air with just a handful of storms.

Still, when I put the historical data together with the larger pattern we’re watching, I’m leaning toward Oklahoma having a better opportunity for above-normal snowfall this winter.

That’s not a prediction that Tulsa will receive 15 or 20 inches of snow. We’re simply too far away to responsibly make a snowfall forecast that specific.

But if you’re asking which direction I would lean right now?

I would lean snowier than normal rather than less snowy than normal.

There are enough pieces on the table to make this winter particularly interesting.

And remember, Oklahoma doesn’t need four straight months of bitter cold to have a big snow season. Sometimes all it takes is a few well-timed storms with cold air already established.

We’ve seen that happen before.

So for the snow lovers who have been waiting for another active Oklahoma winter, I wouldn’t start buying the sleds just yet…

But I also wouldn’t put them too far back in the garage.

items.author: JeffBerardelli
items.text:
🥵 Overheated Holiday Weekend! 
Using the 4-Factor FeelsLike 
Forecast, most cities will peak between 108-114°F.
4 Factors: Temp + Humidity + Sun + Wind. Believe it or not, traditional NOAA heat index forecasts do NOT include the sun and wind. I’ve always thought they should because many folks spend so much time exposed, especially on weekends. So, I found a formula from Dr. Robert Steadman in an old research paper - a version of which is being used by the Australian Bureau of Meteorology right now. Sun spikes it. In sunny spots the sun adds up to 15°. Generally wind cools it. In Florida this time of year there’s lots of sun, but minimal wind so these numbers are 5-10° higher than NOAA’s heat index (in the shade). Bottom line: you can NOT directly compare this to our NOAA traditional heat index, and it should not be used to replace it. It does illustrate how being in the Sun makes a dramatic difference. So… shade is your friend this weekend. Be safe!! #Florida #heat @topfans

HURRICANE MARIE MOISTURE SURGES INTO SW🌧️🌴⚠️Hurricane Marie will remain well offshore, but a plume of its tropical moisture will get pulled north and northeast across parts of the Southwest this Labor Day Weekend. Rain chances begin increasing Saturday, but Sunday looks like the main day for widespread showers, thunderstorms and locally heavy rain from Southern California northeast through the Mojave Desert, southern Nevada, northwestern Arizona and Utah.

Southern California will see increasing tropical moisture Saturday into Sunday. Around Los Angeles, Sunday currently has the greatest rain potential, with most locations expected to receive less than 0.50" and many under 0.25", although locally higher totals are possible in the mountains or beneath heavier showers. San Diego and surrounding areas have a lower overall rainfall signal, but scattered showers remain possible, especially Sunday.

Farther northeast, the moisture plume becomes more impressive. Across southern Nevada, southeastern California and northwestern Arizona, a band of rain is expected to develop Sunday. Current projections generally favor 0.250.50", but locally heavier amounts will be possible depending on exactly where the rain band sets up. Northern Arizona will also see increasing moisture, with Sunday bringing the greatest rain and thunderstorm coverage, especially across northwestern Arizona and near the Grand Canyon.

Utah may end up beneath one of the more favorable setups for heavier rainfall. Tropical moisture interacting with a strong upper-level disturbance should produce widespread, quick-moving showers and thunderstorms Sunday. The Weather Prediction Center has placed a corridor from near Las Vegas and the Grand Canyon northeastward through portions of Utah in the best chance to see excessive rainfall and some flooding, including areas around Zion and Bryce Canyon. Slot canyons, normally dry washes, burn scars and other flood-prone terrain could become particularly dangerous if heavier rain develops.

This does not mean everyone will see heavy rain or that it will rain throughout the entire holiday weekend. Saturday looks more scattered, while Sunday currently has the strongest signal for a broader surge of tropical moisture and locally heavy rainfall. Where heavier showers or thunderstorms develop, localized flash flooding will be possible, especially across the deserts, mountains and slot-canyon country🌧️🌴⚠️

items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text:
MONITORING MARIE | 2 ROUNDS OF MOISTURE🌧️🌴Hurricane Marie is expected to remain well offshore of California, but its tropical moisture could influence parts of the West in multiple waves over the next week! The first push arrives this weekend as moisture from Marie is pulled northward ahead of a trough along the West Coast. Southern California should see increasing clouds and shower chances Saturday into Sunday, with Sunday looking like the wetter day. A few thunderstorms will also be possible, especially across the mountains and deserts. This deeper moisture will spread into southeast California and southern Nevada, into Utah and northern Arizona, bringing an increase in showers and thunderstorms there as well. Farther north across the Great Basin and interior Northwest, additional rain is expected into early next week, although not all of that moisture can necessarily be directly attributed to Marie.

Then attention turns to a possible second push of tropical moisture during the middle to latter part of next week. Forecast confidence is much lower with this round, but there continues to be a signal for another trough to develop over the Eastern Pacific while Marie weakens well offshore. That pattern could potentially draw additional remnant tropical moisture northward into California and portions of the West.

Importantly, this does not mean Marie is forecast to hit California. The circulation itself should remain well offshore and weaken. The story is the moisture being pulled away from the system and transported northward. Exactly how much moisture reaches the West - and where it goes - will depend heavily on the evolution of Marie and the Pacific trough, so the mid-to-late week portion of the forecast remains something to monitor🌧️🌴

items.text:
ACTIVE PATTERN MAY CONTINUE FOR WEST🌧️🌲a persistent trough near the West Coast, combined with an active Eastern Pacific, is expected to favor more opportunities for moisture across a large portion of the West! Tropical moisture could occasionally become involved as well, potentially enhancing rainfall at times. The overall pattern favors above-normal precipitation across much of the West, particularly from the Pacific Northwest and Northern U.S. Rockies southward into parts of the Great Basin and Southwest.

It’s important to remember what a wetter-than-normal outlook actually means. This does not mean it will rain every day, nor does it mean every location will see significant rainfall. The takeaway is the overall signal: the pattern should be more favorable than normal for periodic rain and storm systems across the West, with multiple opportunities for moisture rather than one continuous stretch of wet weather. This wetter signal could persist for a while as troughing remains near the West Coast and Pacific moisture continues to feed into the region🌧️🌲

items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text:
MORE THUNDERSTORMS ACROSS THE NORTHWEST TODAY⛈️a cold upper-level storm system remains over the Pacific Northwest, keeping temperatures unusually cool while creating enough instability for another round of showers and thunderstorms. Across western Washington, showers and isolated thunderstorms will redevelop, particularly near the Cascades, with some activity potentially drifting toward the lowlands. Western Oregon will see increasing thunderstorm chances late this morning and afternoon, especially south of Portland and around the Coast Range and Cascades. Some of the better thunderstorm coverage will extend across southern and central Oregon, including around Bend, before spreading into eastern Oregon and southwest Idaho. Scattered thunderstorms are also possible across eastern Washington, northern Idaho and portions of western Montana.

Severe weather is not the main concern, but stronger cells could produce brief heavy rain, small hail, frequent lightning and locally gusty winds. Storm movement may be slow in some areas, allowing localized heavier rainfall. Given the cold upper low, steep low-level lapse rates and weakly sheared-showery environment, a low-end cold-air funnel is possible, particularly across western Washington and Oregon. Most funnels in this type of environment are brief and remain harmless, although a very small percentage can occasionally reach the ground. Overall, the greatest thunderstorm coverage today should favor Oregon into southwest Idaho⛈️

Check out this photo of a beautiful leucistic ruby-throated hummingbird, spotted in McMinnville, TN. Rick McCulley snapped this awesome photo.

Unlike albino birds, which lack all pigment and have pink or red eyes, leucistic birds carry a genetic condition that reduces feather pigment. That's why this little hummer is nearly all white yet still has dark eyes and a normally colored bill. Sightings like this are extremely rare!

TROPICS | The latest track for #Hurricane #Lowell is out. The new NHC cones still shows a good deal of uncertainty when it comes to how close Lowell will pass to the main islands of Hawaii on Labor Day. 

Right now, the center line is about 300 miles west of Honolulu. This may be close enough to bring some minimal tropical storm winds to O'ahu & stronger gusts on Kauai.   

If the storm center follows the right side of the cone, then winds on Kauai would be much stronger & Honolulu on O'ahu would see weak to moderate tropical storm-force winds, along with rain squalls on Labor Day, as the storm center would then pass about 170 miles to the west.  

On either track, there would be minimal to no impacts in Hilo & the Big Island.  

I'll keep watching the track shifts & will update.

Flash flooding possible today across eastern Arizona and western New Mexico!

A longwave trough over the Pacific Northwest will focus monsoon moisture across the Southwest.
Scattered thunderstorms will develop and propagate northeastward, lowering the flash flood threat for the Tucson metro area. Wet soil conditions from previous storms will promote increased runoff from any heavy rainfall.
Localized flash flooding is possible, specifically across low-lying areas, slot canyons, and burn scars.

items.author: TheWeatherChannel
items.text: Hurricane Hunters are specialized military and civilian aircrews who fly directly into tropical cyclones to gather critical, real-time weather data. Operating highly instrumented aircrafts, they deploy sensors like dropsondes into the eye of the storm to measure wind speed, air pressure, temperature, and humidity from the inside out. This extreme, hands-on data collection provides the precise information needed to build accurate forecasting models, predict a storm's path and intensity, and issue life-saving evacuation warnings.
